title: Marseilles—The Arrival
summary: On 24 February 1815 the ship Pharaon sails into Marseilles under its young mate, Edmond Dantès, whose captain died at sea. The owner, M. Morrel, promises to make him captain, and the supercargo Danglars watches him with jealous hatred.
details: The three-masted merchant ship Pharaon arrives at Marseilles, steered in by a capable nineteen-year-old mate, Edmond Dantès. The shipowner, M. Morrel, rows out to meet her and learns that Captain Leclere died of brain fever on the voyage. The cargo is safe, and Dantès took command himself.

Danglars, the ship's supercargo (the officer in charge of the cargo and accounts), is about twenty-six. He fawns on his bosses, bullies those below him, and the crew dislikes him as much as they love Dantès. He tries to turn Morrel against Dantès, complaining that Dantès lost a day and a half by stopping at the island of Elba. Dantès explains that the dying captain asked him to carry a packet to Marshal Bertrand there. While on Elba he even spoke with the exiled emperor Napoleon, who remembered Morrel's uncle Policar. Morrel quietly approves, but warns that the visit could cause trouble if it became known. Danglars also hints that Leclere gave Dantès a letter, which shows he was eavesdropping at the captain's door.

Morrel invites Dantès to dinner, but Dantès turns him down: he wants to see his father first, and then his fiancée, Mercédès, at the Catalan village. He asks for leave to get married and then travel to Paris. Morrel says he means to make him captain, if he can win over his partner. Asked about Danglars, Dantès admits they quarrelled once (he even proposed settling it on the island of Monte Cristo) but praises his work. As Dantès goes ashore, Morrel and Danglars both watch him leave, with very different expressions.

title: Father and Son
summary: Dantès finds his elderly father half-starved: the old man paid off Edmond's debt to their neighbour Caderousse and lived on almost nothing. The envious Caderousse visits, then reports to Danglars, and the two go off to spy on Dantès and Mercédès.
details: Dantès hurries to his father's small upstairs room in Marseilles. The old man nearly faints for joy. Edmond soon learns that the cupboards are empty. Their neighbour Caderousse demanded repayment of a 140-franc debt Edmond owed him, so his father paid it out of the 200 francs Edmond had left him and lived on sixty francs for three months. Edmond empties his pockets onto the table and promises his father a better life once he is captain.

Caderousse, a tailor of about twenty-five, comes to congratulate Edmond. His friendly words cover envy, and he eyes the money greedily. He teases Edmond for refusing Morrel's dinner invitation and needles him about Mercédès having plenty of admirers. Dantès answers calmly that she will stay faithful, and leaves for the Catalan village.

Outside, Caderousse meets Danglars, who has been waiting for him. He complains that Dantès is 'insolent' about his promotion, and Danglars mutters that if they choose, Dantès may end up even lower than he is now. Caderousse mentions that Mercédès is always seen with a tall, fierce young Catalan she calls her cousin. Sensing a useful rival, Danglars takes Caderousse to La Réserve, an inn near the Catalan village, to drink and watch what happens.

title: The Catalans
summary: In the Catalan village, Mercédès firmly refuses her cousin Fernand, who loves her. Dantès arrives and she forces the two men to shake hands. Fernand runs off and is drawn into drinking with Danglars and Caderousse, and Danglars begins to see a way to ruin Dantès.
details: The Catalans are a close-knit community of Spanish origin living on a point of land outside Marseilles. There, the beautiful young Mercédès turns down yet another proposal from her cousin Fernand, a fisherman. She is a poor orphan and loves him only as a brother, because her heart belongs to Edmond Dantès. When Fernand hints that the sailor may be faithless or dead, she says that if Edmond dies, she will die too.

At that moment Edmond calls from outside and the lovers embrace. Dantès sees Fernand's threatening face, and Fernand's hand goes to his knife. Mercédès says that if any harm comes to Edmond she will throw herself from a cliff, and with a commanding look she makes Fernand shake Edmond's hand. Fernand then rushes out in despair.

Caderousse and Danglars call him into their arbour at the inn. The drunken Caderousse mocks him as a rejected lover while Danglars watches closely. When the happy couple pass by, Dantès announces that the wedding feast will be the next day or the day after, and invites them all, Fernand included. He adds that he must go to Paris afterwards to carry out Captain Leclere's last commission. Danglars realises this means the letter from Elba, and an idea forms in his mind.

title: Conspiracy
summary: Danglars eggs Fernand on, then writes an anonymous letter with his left hand denouncing Dantès as a Bonapartist agent. He pretends it is a joke and throws it away, but Fernand secretly picks it up.
details: Danglars works on Fernand, who admits he would kill Dantès except that Mercédès has sworn to die if Edmond does. Danglars suggests there is no need for murder: prison walls separate lovers as well as a tombstone. The very drunk Caderousse keeps protesting that Dantès is his friend and must not be harmed, so Danglars keeps refilling his glass.

Calling for pen, ink and paper, Danglars points out that Dantès stopped at Elba, where Napoleon was in exile. He writes a denunciation with his left hand so the handwriting cannot be traced, addressed to the king's attorney (the royal prosecutor). It claims that Dantès carried a letter from Murat to 'the usurper' Napoleon, and from Napoleon to the Bonapartist committee in Paris, and that proof will be found on him, at his father's, or in his cabin.

Caderousse, grasping what this means, calls it an infamous shame. Danglars crumples the paper and tosses it into a corner of the arbour, saying it was only a joke. As Danglars leads the staggering Caderousse home, he looks back and sees Fernand pick up the letter, pocket it, and hurry towards the city. Satisfied, Danglars tells himself that the plan will now work on its own.

title: The Marriage Feast
summary: At the joyful feast, Dantès announces that he and Mercédès will marry that very afternoon. Before they can leave, soldiers arrive and arrest him. Morrel returns with the news that the charge is Bonapartist conspiracy, and Danglars frightens Caderousse into silence.
details: The feast is held at La Réserve. Morrel himself attends, which the crew takes as proof that Dantès will be captain. Old Dantès is dressed in his finest. Mercédès seats Fernand beside her as a 'brother', which torments him. Dantès announces that, thanks to Morrel's help, the mayor will marry them at half past two that very day. He will then go to Paris and hold a second celebration on his return.

As the party sets off, a magistrate arrives with soldiers and arrests Dantès 'in the name of the law', giving no reason. Dantès calmly says it must be a mistake and is driven away while Mercédès cries out to him. Fernand slips out and returns pale. Caderousse now remembers the letter and accuses Danglars, who insists he threw it away and blames Fernand. To explain the arrest, Danglars suggests some smuggled goods were found aboard.

Morrel comes back looking grave: Dantès is charged with being a Bonapartist agent. Caderousse wants to confess, but Danglars warns him that anyone who defends Dantès may be treated as his accomplice, and selfish fear wins. Fernand takes Mercédès home. Morrel then hands Danglars temporary command of the Pharaon and goes to plead with M. de Villefort, the deputy prosecutor. Danglars privately rejoices.

title: The Deputy Procureur du Roi
summary: At the same hour, the deputy procureur du roi (the king's deputy prosecutor), Villefort, is celebrating his own betrothal to Renée de Saint-Méran among fierce royalists. We learn his father is the Bonapartist Noirtier. He is called away to deal with the denunciation of Dantès.
details: In an aristocratic mansion in Marseilles, a very different engagement party is under way. The guests are royalists who loathe Napoleon, now exiled on Elba. The Marquis de Saint-Méran toasts King Louis XVIII. His stern wife, the marquise, reminds her future son-in-law, M. de Villefort, that his father was a Girondin (a moderate revolutionary) named Noirtier who later served Napoleon as a senator.

Villefort explains that he has disowned his father's politics and even his name: Noirtier is a Bonapartist, while he is a loyal royalist called de Villefort. The marquise reminds him that the family has vouched for his loyalty to the king, so he must be especially hard on any conspirator. Villefort boasts about the death sentences he has won in court. His gentle fiancée, Renée, is frightened and begs him to be merciful to those she pleads for. The Comte de Salvieux reports that the king himself praised Villefort and approved the match.

A servant calls Villefort out. He returns delighted and reads the anonymous letter accusing Edmond Dantès, which his office opened in the chief prosecutor's absence; the accused is already held at his house. Renée begs him to show mercy on the day of their betrothal. He promises to be lenient if he can, then leaves happily to do his duty.

title: The Examination
summary: Villefort questions Dantès, is convinced he is innocent, and is ready to free him, until he sees that the letter from Elba is addressed to his own father, Noirtier. He burns it and, while pretending to protect Dantès, secretly decides to keep him locked up.
details: Gérard de Villefort, twenty-seven, rich and about to make an advantageous marriage, walks to his office. On the way Morrel begs him to free Dantès, but Villefort, a royalist, treats the shipowner coldly as a suspected Bonapartist.

Dantès is calm and open. He says he is nineteen, has no politics, and loves only his father, Morrel and Mercédès. He does not recognise the handwriting of the denunciation. He explains how the dying Captain Leclere ordered him to take a packet and a ring to the grand-marshal on Elba, who gave him a letter for someone in Paris. Villefort believes him, thinks of pleasing Renée, and tells him he may go once he hands over the letter.

Then he learns the address: M. Noirtier, Rue Coq-Héron, Paris. Villefort turns white and reads the letter three times, fearing that if its contents come out, his connection to Noirtier will ruin him. He asks whether Dantès has shown it to anyone, burns it in the fire, and makes Dantès swear never to mention the letter or the name. Dantès thanks him as a friend. Villefort quietly gives an order to a police agent, then sinks into a chair. He curses his father's past, then smiles: this letter, which could have ruined him, will make his fortune.

title: The Château d’If
summary: Instead of being released, Dantès is taken by boat at night to the Château d'If, a grim island fortress for political prisoners. He begs to see the governor and threatens a jailer, so he is thrown into an underground dungeon.
details: Dantès is held in a cell in the Palais de Justice until about ten at night, still trusting Villefort's promise. Gendarmes then take him by carriage to the harbour and row him out to sea. He passes La Réserve, where the party continues without him, and the Catalan village, where a single light burns in Mercédès' window. Pride stops him from shouting to her.

When a gendarme finally tells him they are going to the Château d'If, Dantès is horrified: there has been no trial and no formalities. He tries to leap overboard but is pinned down at gunpoint. He is locked in a damp cell for the night.

Over the next days he refuses to eat and keeps demanding to see the governor. He bitterly regrets that he did not swim for freedom during the boat trip; he is a famous swimmer and speaks Italian and Spanish. The jailer warns that a former prisoner of the cell, an abbé who kept offering the governor a million francs for his freedom, went mad and was moved to a dungeon. Dantès offers the jailer a hundred crowns to carry a message to Mercédès. When he is refused, he threatens the jailer with a stool. Labelled a madman, he is marched down fifteen steps into a dark dungeon, already close to losing his mind.

title: The Evening of the Betrothal
summary: Villefort rushes to Paris to warn the king of a Napoleonic plot and win the credit himself. He brushes off a pleading Mercédès and feels the first stab of lasting remorse. We see how each of Dantès' friends and enemies spends the night.
details: Back at the Saint-Méran house, Villefort privately tells the marquis that urgent business calls him to Paris. He advises him to sell all his government bonds at once, a hint that he expects political upheaval. He also asks for a letter from the Comte de Salvieux that will get him straight into the king's presence. He refuses to go through the keeper of the seals, because he wants all the credit for his discovery.

At his door he finds Mercédès, who has come to ask about Edmond. Villefort tells her coldly that Dantès is a great criminal and is no longer in his hands. Alone, he is seized by remorse: he has destroyed an innocent man to protect his own ambition. Had Renée or Mercédès pleaded at that moment, he might have signed the release. But only his valet comes in, to announce the carriage, and Villefort leaves. Renée, far from pleading for Dantès, now resents the prisoner whose 'crime' has taken her fiancé away.

Mercédès spends the night in despair with Fernand kneeling at her side. Morrel's appeals to influential friends are refused, since Dantès is now branded a Bonapartist. Caderousse shuts himself in with brandy but cannot drown his conscience. Only Danglars is content, sure of his place on the Pharaon, and he sleeps soundly. Old Dantès waits in agony for news.

title: The King’s Closet at the Tuileries
summary: In Paris, King Louis XVIII teases his anxious adviser Blacas and trusts his complacent police minister. Then Villefort arrives and warns that Napoleon is preparing to leave Elba.
details: In his private study at the Tuileries palace, Louis XVIII annotates his Horace while the Duc de Blacas warns of a storm brewing in the south. The king jokes away his fears. The minister of police, Baron Dandré, reports that Napoleon is bored and possibly going mad on Elba, even telling his old soldiers to 'serve the good king'.

Blacas says that a messenger recommended by M. de Salvieux has raced from Marseilles with alarming news. When the king hears the name Villefort, he grows serious. He knows Villefort's father is Noirtier, the former Girondin and senator, but says the son is so ambitious that he would sacrifice even his father.

Villefort, still dusty from the road, is shown in. He tells the king that Napoleon is arming ships and may already have left Elba, perhaps to land in Italy or France. He claims to have learned this from a Bonapartist sailor he arrested, whom he describes as carrying a spoken message for a Paris Bonapartist whose name he 'could not extract'. He says nothing about the letter or its address. Louis XVIII is confident the coast is well guarded, but promises his gratitude. Just then the minister of police reappears at the door, pale and trembling.

title: The Corsican Ogre
summary: News arrives that Napoleon has landed in France. The king rewards Villefort with the Legion of Honour, but Villefort is shaken when the suspect in a general's murder sounds like his father, and then that very man turns up at his hotel.
details: Dandré confesses that Napoleon left Elba on 26 February and landed near Antibes on 1 March, and that he is advancing by way of Gap and Sisteron. The king learns this only on 3 March, by telegraph, and is furious and humiliated. He contrasts his whole police force with the single magistrate who foresaw it. Villefort shrewdly defends the minister, earning his gratitude, partly because a desperate minister might question Dantès and uncover the truth.

The king then asks about the death of General Quesnel, a royalist who disappeared after being lured to a Bonapartist club in the Rue Saint-Jacques. The police now think he was murdered, not a suicide. They describe the suspect: about fifty, dark, with black whiskers, a blue frock-coat buttoned to the chin and the rosette of the Legion of Honour, last seen near the Rue Coq-Héron. Villefort nearly collapses, then breathes again when he hears the man escaped.

The king pointedly asks whether he has visited his father, then gives him his own Legion of Honour cross. Back at his hotel, Villefort is told that a stranger matching the police description is asking for him. The visitor walks in and greets him as 'my dear Gérard'. It is his father.

title: Father and Son
summary: Noirtier, a leading Bonapartist, calmly admits his role in the club linked to General Quesnel's death and predicts Napoleon will reach Paris within weeks. He shaves off his whiskers to disguise himself and walks out past the police.
details: Noirtier locks the doors and teases his son for being in Paris instead of at his wedding. Villefort says he came to save him. Noirtier coolly confirms that he is vice-president of the Bonapartist club at No. 53 Rue Saint-Jacques. Villefort explains that he intercepted a letter from Elba addressed to Noirtier and burned it, because it would have got his father shot and ruined his own career.

Noirtier gives his own account of General Quesnel. The club believed he was on their side and told him the whole plan for Napoleon's return. Quesnel said he was a royalist, swore an oath of silence, was 'allowed to depart free', and 'lost his way'. Noirtier insists that in politics there are no murders, only obstacles removed. He predicts that Napoleon will be at Grenoble, then Lyons, and in Paris by around the 20th, welcomed rather than resisted, and proves how good his own network is by having found his son within half an hour of his arrival.

When Villefort repeats the police description, Noirtier shaves off his black whiskers and puts on his son's brown coat and hat. He tells Gérard to go home quietly and keep his head down, promising to protect him in return. He strolls past the agents watching the street. Villefort hides his father's clothes, burns the cane, and hurries back to Marseilles, hearing on the way that Napoleon has entered Grenoble.

title: The Hundred Days
summary: During Napoleon's brief return to power, Villefort tricks Morrel into writing a petition that makes Dantès look like a dangerous Bonapartist, and keeps it. After Waterloo, Dantès is forgotten in prison, his enemies move on, and his father dies.
details: Napoleon retakes the throne. Noirtier's influence protects Villefort's post, and Villefort postpones his marriage until he sees which side will win. With Bonapartists now in favour, Morrel asks what has become of Dantès. Villefort coolly pretends to look him up in the register, claims he was sent off to some distant fortress, and explains that some prisoners are made to vanish without records. He then 'helps' Morrel write a petition to the minister. It praises Dantès as one of the most active agents of Napoleon's return, and Villefort certifies it.

Instead of sending it, Villefort keeps the petition, which would be damning if the king returned. After Waterloo, Louis XVIII is restored. Villefort becomes king's prosecutor at Toulouse and marries Renée de Saint-Méran. Dantès stays in his dungeon, forgotten by everyone.

Danglars, afraid Dantès might return for revenge, gets a recommendation from Morrel and goes to Madrid to work for a Spanish merchant, and nothing more is heard of him. Fernand broods over plans to kill Dantès and himself, then is called up in Napoleon's last conscription. Mercédès, grateful for his kindness, sends him off calling him her brother, which gives him hope. Caderousse, married and older, is sent to the frontier. Old Dantès loses all hope when Napoleon falls and dies in Mercédès' arms five months after his son's arrest. Morrel bravely pays for the funeral, even though helping a 'Bonapartist's' father is dangerous.

title: The Two Prisoners
summary: In July 1816 a prison inspector visits the dungeons. Dantès humbly begs for a trial, and the inspector promises to look into it. In another cell, the 'mad' Abbé Faria offers millions for his freedom. A note in Dantès' file dooms his hopes.
details: A year after the king's return, an inspector-general of prisons tours the Château d'If with the governor. He is shown the 'dangerous' prisoner who once attacked the turnkey Antoine. Dantès, now subdued, asks only to know his crime and be tried. He was arrested on 28 February 1815, and it is now 30 July 1816: seventeen months, which to him feel like seventeen ages. He names Villefort as the man who arrested him and calls him kind. Moved, the inspector promises to examine his case.

Next they visit No. 27, the Abbé Faria, an Italian priest imprisoned since 1811 and thought to have gone mad in 1813. He is found drawing geometry on the floor of his cell. Faria says he was secretary to Cardinal Spada for twenty years and was arrested at Piombino. He dreamed of a united Italy. He asks to speak privately about a huge treasure and offers five, then six, millions for his liberty, promising to stay in prison while they check. The officials laugh it off as the familiar madness.

The inspector finds a note in Dantès' file, written in a different hand and added after he was locked up: 'Violent Bonapartist; took an active part in the return from Elba.' It echoes the petition Villefort kept. The inspector writes 'Nothing to be done.' Dantès, newly hopeful, starts marking the days on the wall, but months pass with no change. A new governor arrives who knows prisoners only by number, and Dantès becomes simply 'number 34'.

title: Number 34 and Number 27
summary: After years of despair, Dantès tries to starve himself to death, until he hears someone digging behind his wall. He starts tunnelling towards the sound, and finally the other prisoner, No. 27, breaks through into his cell.
details: Dantès goes through every stage of a prisoner's suffering: pride, doubt, pleading, prayer, then rage against the unknown enemies who wrote the letter. He finally decides to die by starving himself, secretly throwing his food out of the window. Nearly four years in, close to death, he hears a scraping sound inside the wall.

Hope returns. Dantès eats again, knocks to test whether the noise is a workman or a prisoner, and concludes from the cautious silence that it is a fellow captive. With a shard of a broken jug and then the iron handle of the soup saucepan, which he tricks the jailer into leaving, he digs out a stone. He reflects that he has wasted six years in prison when he could have been working like this.

When a beam blocks his way and he cries out to God in despair, a voice answers from below. The stranger has been in prison since 1811 and has never heard of Napoleon's fall. He explains that he was digging towards the sea but miscalculated and reached the wrong wall. He gives his name only as 'No. 27' and is wary, but is reassured by Dantès' age and sincerity. Dantès, who was nineteen at his arrest and is now not quite twenty-six, begs not to be abandoned, offering to love him like a father. The next day the floor gives way and an old man climbs up into his cell.

title: A Learned Italian
summary: The newcomer is the Abbé Faria, a brilliant Italian scholar. He has made his own tools, pens, ink and paper, and has written a whole book in prison. His escape plan has failed, but his determination inspires Dantès to suggest a new one.
details: The stranger is small, about sixty, with white hair and a long black beard. He shows Dantès a chisel made from a bed clamp, which he used to dig the fifty-foot tunnel. Climbing onto Dantès' shoulders, he sees that the window looks onto a gallery patrolled by soldiers, so escape through this cell is impossible. He introduces himself as the Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811. He was jailed for dreaming of uniting Italy and was betrayed by a ruler he trusted. He admits he is the 'mad priest' of the Château d'If.

Faria accepts the failure as God's will, but his example fires Dantès with fresh courage: if this old man could do so much, a young, strong swimmer could do more. Dantès proposes cutting a side tunnel into the gallery and killing the sentry. Faria refuses to shed blood. He prefers to wait patiently for a lucky chance, as in history's famous escapes.

Dantès is amazed to learn what Faria has done alone in his cell. He has written a treatise on a united Italian monarchy on strips of linen made smooth by a chemical process. He makes pens from fish cartilage and ink from soot and wine, and writes in his own blood for important notes. He knows some 150 books by heart and speaks five modern languages. Eager to see it all, Dantès follows him into the tunnel.

title: The Abbé’s Chamber
summary: Faria shows Dantès that Danglars and Fernand denounced him and that Villefort buried him to protect his father, Noirtier. Dantès swears revenge. Faria educates him, and they dig an escape tunnel until a fit leaves Faria paralysed.
details: In his own cell Faria tells the time by the sun, and shows his linen manuscript, his fish-bone pens, his knives, a lamp made from melted fat, and a rope ladder. Dantès tells his story. Faria applies a simple rule: look for whoever gains from the crime. Danglars wanted the captaincy, overheard Captain Leclere and saw the letter. Fernand wanted Mercédès. Dantès remembers seeing them with Caderousse and pen, ink and paper at the inn the day before his wedding. Faria writes with his left hand to show how the accusation's handwriting was disguised.

Then Faria questions him about the deputy prosecutor who burned the letter. Hearing the names Noirtier and Villefort, he laughs and explains that Noirtier was Villefort's father. Stunned, Dantès goes back to his cell and swears a solemn oath of vengeance. Faria regrets having planted that passion in him.

Dantès asks to be taught, and Faria teaches him mathematics, history, science and languages. Within a year Dantès is a new man, cultivated and polished. Faria finally agrees to an escape plan as long as the sentry is harmed only as a last resort. For fifteen months they tunnel beneath the gallery.

On the eve of escape, Faria is struck by a seizure. Following his instructions, Dantès gives him drops of a red remedy, and he revives. But his right arm and leg are paralysed. He warns that a third attack, like the ones that killed his father and grandfather, will kill him. He urges Dantès to flee alone, but Dantès swears never to leave him while he lives.

title: The Treasure
summary: Faria reveals his secret: a half-burnt letter from 1498 in which Cardinal Spada describes a vast treasure hidden in the caves of the island of Monte Cristo. Faria names Dantès as his heir and calls him his son.
details: Faria shows Dantès a scorched paper and says it is his treasure, half of which now belongs to Dantès. Dantès fears the illness has made Faria truly mad and avoids him. That evening the paralysed abbé drags himself through the tunnel to tell his story.

Faria served the last Count of Spada, a descendant of a noble Roman family once said to be fabulously rich. In 1498, Pope Alexander VI and his son Cæsar Borgia made Cardinal Cæsar Spada and Cardinal Rospigliosi buy their posts, then invited them to dinner and poisoned them in order to seize their wealth. But Spada's fortune was never found. His will left his nephew only his papers and his gold-cornered breviary (prayer book). For three centuries the family searched in vain.

When the last count died, he left Faria his library and the breviary. In 1807, lighting a candle with an old bookmark from the breviary, Faria saw writing appear in the heat: invisible ink. With a second fragment he reconstructed the message. Spada had buried all his gold, jewels and gems, nearly two million Roman crowns, in the caves of the little island of Monte Cristo, to be found by raising the twentieth rock from a small creek to the east, in the furthest corner of the second opening. Faria was arrested as he set out to find it. The family is now extinct, so the treasure is his to give. Dantès protests that he is no relation, but Faria declares him 'the child of my captivity', and Dantès weeps on his neck.

title: The Third Attack
summary: Their tunnel is blocked when the gallery is rebuilt, and Faria prepares Dantès to recover the treasure alone. One night the third attack comes. Despite the remedy, Faria dies, and Dantès overhears the jailers planning to dispose of the body that evening.
details: Faria talks constantly of the good the fortune could do. Dantès, remembering his oath, thinks instead of the harm it could do to his enemies. Dantès knows Monte Cristo, a deserted, cone-shaped rock between Corsica and Elba, and draws a map for Faria. Then the ruined sea gallery is rebuilt and their escape route is sealed. Dantès tells Faria that his real treasure is their friendship and all the knowledge Faria has given him. Faria makes him learn Spada's letter by heart, destroys the second fragment, and coaches him on how to reach the island and search it.

One night Dantès wakes to hear Faria calling. The old man is seized by the fatal attack. He stops Dantès from calling for help, so that their secret will not be discovered, blesses him as his son, and tells him to hurry to Monte Cristo. His last words are 'Monte Cristo, forget not Monte Cristo!' Dantès gives him twelve drops, then the rest of the phial, but by dawn Faria is dead.

Hidden in the tunnel, Dantès hears the jailers mock 'the madman' and his treasure. The doctor confirms the death with a hot iron to the heel. The jailer recalls that Faria once cured his wife's illness. The governor orders the body sewn into a sack, without a mass, since the chaplain is away, and removed between ten and eleven that night. When the cell is empty, Dantès climbs out into it.

title: The Cemetery of the Château d’If
summary: Dantès takes his dead friend's place in the burial sack, planning to escape from the grave. Instead, the jailers tie a cannonball to his feet and fling him off the cliffs into the sea.
details: Sitting beside the sack that holds Faria's body, Dantès is tempted by suicide, then passes from despair to a fierce will to live, punish his enemies, and reward any friends. A thought strikes him: only the dead leave this place freely, so he will take the dead man's place.

Using Faria's homemade knife, he opens the sack and carries the body through the tunnel to his own bed, arranging it to look as if he is asleep with his face to the wall. He takes Faria's needle and thread, climbs into the sack naked and sews it shut from inside. He plans to slit the sack and fight his way out if he is discovered, or to dig himself out of the grave once the gravediggers leave.

The jailer's seven o'clock visit passes without trouble. Late that night two men carry the sack out into the windy night, joking that the old man is heavy. They stop, tie something heavy to his feet with a cord, and carry him up some steps while the waves crash below, joking that it is no night for a swim. They swing him, 'One! two! three!', and throw him into the air. Weighted with a thirty-six-pound cannonball, Dantès plunges into the icy sea. The sea, it turns out, is the cemetery of the Château d'If.

title: The Island of Tiboulen
summary: Dantès cuts himself free, swims through a storm to a barren islet, and is rescued by Genoese smugglers, posing as a shipwrecked Maltese sailor. It is 28 February 1829, fourteen years to the day since his arrest, and he renews his vow of revenge.
details: With the knife in his hand, Dantès slashes open the sack, cuts the cord holding the cannonball, and surfaces, diving again to avoid the torch-bearing gravediggers above. Steering by the Planier lighthouse, he swims for over an hour through rough sea and reaches the rocky islet of Tiboulen, where he collapses asleep. A violent storm breaks. By lightning he sees a fishing boat smash on the rocks and its crew drown.

At dawn, knowing the alarm will soon be raised at the fortress, he spots a Genoese tartan (a small Mediterranean sailing vessel) leaving Marseilles. He guesses its crew are smugglers. He puts on a drowned sailor's red cap, grabs a piece of wreckage and swims to cut across the boat's course. He is close to drowning when a sailor hauls him aboard by the hair.

He claims to be a Maltese sailor from last night's wreck. He explains his long hair and beard as a religious vow, then proves his skill by steering the boat flawlessly. The captain agrees to take him on. Jacopo, the sailor who saved him, lends him clothes. When the alarm gun fires from the Château d'If, Dantès calmly says a prisoner must have escaped and goes on sipping his rum. Jacopo tells him the date: 28 February 1829. Arrested at nineteen, Dantès is now thirty-three. He wonders what has become of Mercédès, and renews his oath of vengeance against Danglars, Fernand and Villefort as the tartan races towards Leghorn (Livorno).

title: The Smugglers
summary: Dantès sails with the smugglers of La Jeune Amélie, sees his transformed face in a mirror, is wounded in a skirmish with customs officers, and teaches the loyal Jacopo navigation. At last the smugglers choose Monte Cristo as a meeting place for their next job.
details: The master of La Jeune Amélie, a Genoese smuggler, comes to trust his skilled and tight-lipped recruit, though he never learns who Dantès really is. At Leghorn, Dantès has his hair and beard cut and sees himself for the first time in fourteen years. His open, smiling young face has become pale, stern and thoughtful, with eyes that can see in the dark and a changeable voice. No one who once knew him could recognise him. He signs on for three months only.

They run contraband to Corsica and Sardinia. On one run he passes close to Monte Cristo but has no chance to land. In a fight with customs men off the coast of Lucca, a customs officer is killed and Dantès is shot in the shoulder. He bears it calmly, and notices that the officer's death barely moves him: his heart is hardening. Jacopo, a Corsican, nurses him devotedly and indignantly refuses a share of his money, so Dantès grows fond of him and teaches him navigation and the stars, just as Faria once taught him.

After two and a half months Dantès has learned the smugglers' trade, their contacts and their secret signs, and has saved a hundred piastres. He plans to hire a boat of his own, but cannot find a way to search the island without companions. Then, at a smugglers' tavern in Leghorn, the master proposes the deserted island of Monte Cristo as a neutral place to exchange a valuable cargo. Dantès hides his joy and agrees they should sail the next night.

title: The Island of Monte Cristo
summary: On Monte Cristo, Dantès secretly finds carved marks on the rocks, then fakes a bad fall so the smugglers will leave him behind with a gun and a pickaxe. As soon as they sail out of sight, he springs up and heads for the treasure.
details: After a feverish night of dreams about jewelled caves, Dantès steers La Jeune Amélie to Monte Cristo. The crew call him 'the Maltese' and obey him almost like a commander, and the old master sees him as his natural successor. He is the first to leap ashore. He is shaken when Jacopo says there are no caves on the island, but decides the entrances must have been blocked up.

The next day, pretending to hunt wild goats, he sends Jacopo back with a kid for the cooks. Exploring alone, he finds marks carved by human hands on the rocks. They lead to a large round boulder, then seem to stop. Looking down at his comrades, he reflects that they will happily risk their lives for a few piastres, while he hopes for far more.

Running back when they signal that the meal is ready, he slips and falls down a slope. He claims to be in agony with a hurt knee and, the master suspects, broken ribs, and refuses to be moved. The master, Captain Baldi, must sail to deliver his cargo. Jacopo offers to give up his share and stay to nurse him, but Dantès insists on being left alone with biscuits, a gun, powder and a pickaxe, asking them to send a fishing boat or come back for him in a week.

He watches the tartan sail away, marvelling that he has found true friendship among such men. Once it is out of sight, Dantès leaps up as nimbly as a goat, takes his gun and pickaxe, and hurries to the rock where the marks ended, crying, like the fisherman in Faria's Arabian tale, 'Open Sesame!'
